content: Cancer remains one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide. Treatments for gynecological cancers, in particular, can significantly affect a patient’s quality of life (QoL). Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) refer to self-reported assessments by patients regarding their health status and overall well-being. These measures encompass a variety of tools but are specifically designed to capture the patient’s perspective. Utilizing QoL and cancer-specific questionnaires as alternatives to traditional follow-up methods may provide substantial psychological benefits for patients while also offering potential cost savings for healthcare systems. The primary objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of PROMs as a substitute for routine follow-up in women who have undergone treatment for gynecological cancers. Specifically, the study aimed to determine whether PROMs could effectively identify cancer recurrences, influence overall survival rates, and provide psychological benefits to patients. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), with the search extending up to November 2012. Additional sources, such as clinical trial registries, abstracts from scientific meetings, and reference lists from review articles, were also examined. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies with concurrent comparison groups. These studies needed to be of sufficient quality, employing statistical adjustments for baseline differences using multivariable analyses. The analysis included studies where women completed PROMs at regular intervals and submitted their results for evaluation by their cancer care team, as well as studies involving structured interviews during follow-up. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of the identified studies. Despite an extensive search that yielded 2524 unique references, no studies met the inclusion criteria. Consequently, no data were available for analysis. The authors concluded that there is currently no evidence to support or refute the use of PROMs as a follow-up strategy for women treated for gynecological cancers. To address this gap, future research should focus on well-designed RCTs, preferably conducted across multiple centers or countries, or robust non-randomized studies that utilize multivariable analyses to account for baseline differences. Such studies are essential to compare follow-up strategies and enhance the current understanding of the role of PROMs in this context.
